title: Bài sưu tầm 206 - Passage 2: Nature’s Sticky Secret: The Science of Dry Adhesion
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 206

Nature’s Sticky Secret: The Science of Dry Adhesion

Paragraph A. For over two millennia, natural philosophers and zoologists were baffled by the locomotion of the gecko. Aristotle famously remarked in the fourth century BCE that the agile lizard could 'run up and down a tree in any way, even with the head downwards.' Unlike tree frogs that rely on capillary action from liquid mucus, or insects equipped with mechanical claws that grip microscopic surface crevices, the gecko walks effortlessly across polished ceilings and wet glass without expending metabolic energy or leaving any chemical residue behind. For centuries, this astonishing feat was attributed to electrostatic attraction, suction pads, or microscopic hooks. Only in the twenty-first century did nanotechnology and advanced electron microscopy finally unlock the physical principles governing this natural marvel.

Paragraph B. The biological mechanism of gecko adhesion is entirely mechanical and physical. A gecko's toe pads feature millions of microscopic keratin hairs termed setae, each roughly one-tenth the diameter of a human hair. Under an electron microscope, each individual seta branches into hundreds of even tinier flattened tips called spatulae. When these compliant nanoscale spatulae come into intimate physical contact with a substrate, the atomic gaps between the two surfaces narrow to less than a nanometre. At this scale, weak intermolecular forces known as van der Waals interactions arise between adjacent molecules. While an individual van der Waals interaction is negligible, the collective surface contact achieved by billions of spatulae produces extraordinary adhesive strength, capable of supporting up to fifty times the lizard’s body weight.

Paragraph C. However, static adhesion alone is useless for an agile creature; an animal permanently glued to a wall would quickly starve. 'The genius of the gecko is not merely that it sticks, but that it unhooks instantly,' explains Dr. Ronald Fearing, a biomechanical engineer at the University of California, Berkeley. 'Gecko adhesion is direction-dependent. When the lizard drags its foot downward and inward along a vertical surface, the setae align at a shallow angle, activating maximum intermolecular contact. But the moment the gecko rolls its toes upward, the angle alters, the contact area collapses, and the foot releases effortlessly.' This directional asymmetry allows geckos to achieve running speeds exceeding one metre per second across vertical walls.

Paragraph D. Translating this biological masterpiece into commercial synthetic adhesives proved immensely challenging. Early synthetic variants constructed from silicone or polyurethane deteriorated rapidly because the microscopic artificial hairs clustered together and tangled when subjected to mechanical pressure. Dr. Kellar Autumn, a pioneering biophysicist, led an experimental project fabricating dry adhesives using carbon nanotubes. Autumn’s team molded arrays of dense, vertically aligned nanotubes onto flexible polymer backings. In laboratory trials, these synthetic patches supported remarkable shear loads while functioning flawlessly inside vacuum chambers and at temperatures below minus one hundred degrees Celsius—conditions where chemical glues freeze, become brittle, and lose all adhesive capability.

Paragraph E. The medical sector has emerged as one of the most enthusiastic early adopters of gecko-inspired biomaterials. Dr. Maria Delgado, a surgical researcher, has pioneered the development of bio-compatible dry adhesive tape designed for internal incisions. Traditional surgical sutures and staples can puncture delicate internal tissues, causing localized trauma, inflammation, and potential bodily fluid leaks. Delgado’s adhesive tape, synthesized from biodegradable polyglycerol sebacate, bonds securely to moist organ surfaces via physical nano-patterns without evoking an immune response. In clinical trials on vascular repairs, the gecko-inspired tape sealed arterial incisions thirty percent faster than conventional suturing, dissolving harmlessly once the natural tissue regenerated.

Paragraph F. Beyond medicine, aerospace engineers are deploying dry adhesives to solve one of the most dangerous operational hazards in modern orbit: space debris. Dr. Hiroshi Tanaka, an autonomous robotics specialist, cautions that traditional docking methods fail in the zero-gravity vacuum of space. Suction cups are inoperable because there is no atmospheric pressure, while chemical glues degrade under intense solar radiation and outgas toxic chemicals into satellite mechanisms. Tanaka’s team developed robotic gripper pads fitted with gecko-patterned adhesives. In orbital tests, robotic arms equipped with these grippers succeeded in grasping tumbling rocket upper stages and defunct satellites smoothly, exerting gentle, non-destructive contact that prevents objects from bouncing away into deeper orbits.

Paragraph G. Looking toward domestic and industrial manufacturing, scientists emphasize that synthetic dry adhesives offer a profound environmental advantage. Chemical glues and epoxy resins are notorious for complicating the recycling of electronics and automobiles; separating glued components requires toxic organic solvents or intense heat, destroying valuable raw materials in the process. Dr. Ronald Fearing envisions an industrial paradigm where smartphones, vehicle panels, and consumer appliances are assembled entirely with directional dry adhesives. At the end of a product's operating lifecycle, a simple mechanical peeling motion could disassemble components in seconds, facilitating closed-loop, zero-waste recycling.

steps: Đoạn G: "a simple mechanical peeling motion could disassemble components in seconds, facilitating closed-loop, zero-waste recycling."

steps: Đoạn A: "attributed to electrostatic attraction, suction pads, or microscopic hooks."

q17.text: details of how medical adhesives avoid the damage caused by traditional surgical methods

steps: Đoạn E: "traditional surgical sutures and staples can puncture delicate internal tissues, causing localized trauma... Delgado’s adhesive tape... bonds securely without evoking an immune response."

Đoạn D: "...supported remarkable shear loads..." (Distractors: forces, patches).
Đoạn D: "...where chemical glues freeze, become brittle..." (Distractors: resins, adhesives).

q22.text: Standard suction devices cannot be used in space because there is an absence of air pressure.

steps: Đoạn F (Dr. Hiroshi Tanaka): "Suction cups are inoperable because there is no atmospheric pressure..."

q23.text: The gecko’s climbing agility depends on its ability to alter adhesive contact based on foot direction.

steps: Đoạn C (Dr. Ronald Fearing): "The genius of the gecko is not merely that it sticks, but that it unhooks instantly... Gecko adhesion is direction-dependent."

q24.text: Gecko-inspired adhesives could replace chemical fasteners to facilitate the easy disassembly of consumer products.

steps: Đoạn G (Dr. Ronald Fearing): "Dr. Ronald Fearing envisions an industrial paradigm where smartphones, vehicle panels... are assembled entirely with directional dry adhesives."

q25.text: Traditional metal staples and stitches can cause tissue trauma and leaks during surgical procedures.

steps: Đoạn E (Dr. Maria Delgado): "Traditional surgical sutures and staples can puncture delicate internal tissues, causing localized trauma..."

q26.text: Robotic capturing mechanisms equipped with dry adhesives can secure orbital objects without causing them to ricochet.
